title: Fitting shapes into holes
keyIdea: Each shape fits the hole that matches it: round in round, square in square, triangle in triangle. If a shape is the right one but will not go in, turn it until its straight sides and corners line up with the hole. A circle has no corners, so it fits any way round, and it is the shape that rolls.

kid: Look at the shape. Now look at the holes. Find the hole that looks the same. Round goes in round. Square goes in square.
Bump! The triangle will not go in. Do not push. Turn it round and round. When the corners line up, it drops in. Plop!
A corner is a pointy bit. A square has 4 corners. A triangle has 3. A circle has none. It is round all the way.
Round things roll. Put a ball on a slope and it rolls away. A block has flat sides, so it stops.
adult: Fitting pieces into a shape sorter or inset puzzle is one of the first geometry tasks for two and three year olds. To do it, a child must match the outline of a piece to the outline of a hole, notice straight edges, corners and curves, and turn the piece until it lines up. This early spatial thinking supports later work on naming 2D shapes and their properties.

At first most toddlers use trial and error: they push a piece at every hole. With practice they start to look before they try, pick the matching hole, and rotate the piece in the hand before it gets there. You can help by naming what they feel: straight side, pointy corner, round edge.

Common mistakes to watch for: pushing harder instead of turning the piece; trying a square in the rectangle hole because both have four corners; and thinking a turned triangle is a different shape. Show that it is the same triangle, just turned. A circle fits any way round, a square fits four ways, and a triangle three ways, because of how their corners repeat.

In the lab your child drags a circle, a square and a triangle into a sorter, turns an upside-down triangle until it drops in, turns a standing rectangle so it lies flat, lets shapes go on a slope to see which one rolls, sorts shapes into corners and no corners, and fills the sorter with turned pieces.

familyTip: Use a real shape sorter or cut shapes from a cereal box and draw round them to make holes. When a piece will not go in, say "Let's turn it" rather than doing it for them. At bath time, ask which toys roll and which slide.

visual.caption: Corners or no corners? Drag each shape, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match shapes to holes, turn pieces until they fit, roll shapes down a slope and sort corners from curves.

practice.prompt: Which hole does a round circle fit?
practice.hint: Look for the hole with no pointy corners.
practice.explain: A circle fits the round hole. It has no corners, so it needs a hole with no corners.

practice.prompt: Ava has {n} triangles. One will not go in its hole. What should she do?
practice.hint: Is it the right shape? Then the corners must line up.
practice.explain: Turn it until the corners line up with the hole. All {n} triangles fit once they are turned the right way.

practice.prompt: How many corners does a square have?
practice.hint: Touch each pointy bit and count.
practice.explain: A square has 4 corners and 4 straight sides. A triangle has 3 corners, and a circle has none.

practice.prompt: Sam puts {n} shapes on a slope. Which one rolls away?
practice.hint: Which shape is round all the way, with no flat side to stop it?
practice.explain: The ball rolls. Of Sam's {n} shapes, only the round one has no flat side or corner to stop it.

pool.hint: Count the pointy bits on each shape.
pool.explain: A triangle has 3 corners and 3 straight sides. A square has 4 corners and a circle has none.

pool.prompt: The square will not go in the round hole. Why?
pool.hint: What does a square have that a round hole does not?
pool.explain: The square has corners and straight sides. The round hole has no corners, so the square needs the square hole.

pool.prompt: Which shape fits any way you turn it?
pool.hint: Which shape looks the same however you turn it?
pool.explain: A circle fits any way round. It is round all the way, so there are no corners to line up.

pool.prompt: A long rectangle is standing up. Its hole lies flat. What do you do?
choices: Put it in the square hole
pool.hint: Make the piece look like the hole.
pool.explain: Turn the rectangle so it lies flat like the hole. The square hole is too short for it.

pool.prompt: Leo fits {n} round pieces in a row. Which hole did they go in?
pool.hint: Round pieces match a hole with the same round edge.
pool.explain: All {n} round pieces go in the round hole. Round fits round.

pool.hint: Run your finger round the edge. Do you feel a pointy bit?
pool.explain: An oval is curved all the way round, like an egg, so it has no corners.

pool.prompt: Mia puts {n} blocks on a slope. They do not roll. Why not?
pool.hint: What stops a block? Look at its sides and corners.
pool.explain: All {n} blocks have flat sides and corners, so they slide or stop. Round things roll.
